I'm trying to adjust raw counts of lemurs. My goal is to calculate a N_k.=

ty

> > really.  Either way, your GLM or GAM will no longer have a Poisson erro=
r=20
> > term as the response variable is non-integer -- perhaps a Gamma?=20
> >
> > 3. Retain the n_k as the response variable in a Poisson model, but use=20=

> > pi*nu_k^2 as an offset, where nu_k is the effective detection radius fo=
r=20
> > that point.
> >
> > Personally, I prefer 3 as you get to keep the discrete nature of the=20=

> > counts.  However method 3 doesn't work if you have any species level=20=

=20

h=20

> > that says how to calculate p_i for each animal given the parameter=20
> > estimates of the detection function.

I, unfortunately, have the added complication of having clusters of lemur=
s.
 So, my understanding from above, is that I cannot simply divide n_k by p=
_k?
 Instead, I'll need to calculate p_i for each lemur detected at the point=
?=20=20

I checked the online manual and found the section in Chpt. 8 entitled
"Calculating probability of detection" and think that is the section you
were referring to above.=20=20

My questions are: 1) Can I simply divide n_k by p_k to get N_k?

If not, 2) in the formula mentioned above (p. 94 User's Guide), is distan=
ce
y the actual distance to each individual in the group?  And is y_s the

Thanks for your help!

Cheers,
Anne Axel

messages.subject: Re: correcting inflated estimates
messages.body_plain:
Carol, I don't think you can assume that the problem is
double-counting.  If there is much bird movement during the 5-min
counts, then it may be new birds moving onto the plot and being
detected.  Or it may just be that birds already on the plot but not
detected in the first minute are detected witnin 5 mins.  From the data
alone, you cannot tell which method is the less biased.  I would expect
in most circumstances 1-min counts to lead to underestimates of
abundance unless the habitat is very open, due to failure to detect all
birds near the point in the first minute.  In closed habitats, 5-min
counts might yield underestimates too, for the same reason.  But in the
presence of bird movement, they might lead to overestimation of density,
whether or not double-counting occurs.

I don't think that you should attempt to compare estimates from 5-min
counts with ones from 1-min counts.  If more data are to be collected, I
would rethink the study design, so that these problems can be avoided in
future.  We advocate a 'snapshot' approach - I describe this approach,
and compare it with 5-min counts, in

Buckland, S.T. 2006.  Point transect surveys for songbirds:  robust
methodologies.  /The Auk/ *123*, 345-357.

Steve Buckland

Carol Rizkalla wrote:
> > First, I apologize if this has already been answered - perhaps I used the
> > wrong search terms in the archive.
> >
> > I'm new to the bird world, and have inherited a point count dataset which
> > I've just analyzed. The first two years, 5 minute counts were conducted in
> > the winter and summer at a set of points. The last 3 years, five 1 minute
> > counts were conducted at each point.
> >
> > The estimates show that density is twice as high in winter than in summer,
> > which we expect. However, the estimates from the first two years are twice
> > as high again.
> >
> > eg. Winter 2004 D = 15.5, SE = 1.8        Winter 2006 D = 8.6, SE = 0.9
> >     Summer 2004 D = 9.4, SE = 1.8         Summer 2006 D = 4.9, SE = 0.5
> >
> > I suspect that there was double counting due to bird movement in the 5 min
> > counts, but there is no way to confirm this from the raw data.
> > Detection functions seem fine and all models are a good fit.
> >
> > I thought that including species as a factor in the detection function
> > brings would help. For winter 2004, it's a better model by AIC, D is
> > lower, but there are 40 parameters and a poor fit. For summer 2004, it's
> > also a better model with poor fit, but really no change in D.
> >
> > So I'm not sure if there is another way to correct for double counting.
> >
> > Thanks in advance for any advice.
> >
> > Carol

messages.subject: Re: multispecies sampling
messages.body_plain:
Urbain-

I believe your post contains 2 aspects.  The first is about differences=20
in detectability (g(x)) for species or groups of species.  You can=20
easily accommodate those differences using species or species size=20
(large,medium,small) as a factor variable using the MCDS or MRDS=20
analysis engines in DISTANCE.  The second aspect is in regards to=20
design. This is a more difficult question.  It is rarely possible to=20
have a single design that is optimal for several species.  To get the=20
best precision for a particular species, you want to stratify the survey=20
and put the most effort in the strata with highest abundance.  Trying to=20
do this with several species is difficult because the areas of highest=20
densities usually differ for the species.  Thus, I'm afraid you will=20
have to stay with a single survey design although you may be able to add=20
lines to improve precision for species of particular interest.  Also,=20
spatial modelling may help improve precision.

regards --jeff

messages.subject: Bootstrapping with Poststratification by Species
messages.body_plain:
Dear List

I conducted multi-species bird point surveys on 20 different sites (no. of
points from 10-15) with the aim of obtaining density estimates for each
species at each site.  Even with detections pooled across sites there were
not sufficient detections for all species, so I have grouped species of
similar detectability into small groups (2-3 species).  To obtain density
estimates I have tried two methods.

1) Using the CDS engine, I used a filter to select a group, with the
detection function fitted at a global level and density estimates at the

messages.subject: Bootstrapping with Poststratification by Species
messages.body_plain:
Dear List

I conducted multi-species bird point surveys on 20 different sites (no. of
points from 10-15) with the aim of obtaining density estimates for each
species at each site.  Even with detections pooled across sites there were
not sufficient detections for all species, so I have grouped species of
similar detectability into small groups (2-3 species).  To obtain density
estimates I have tried two methods.

1) Using the CDS engine, I used a filter to select a group, with the
detection function fitted at a global level and density estimates at the
sample(point) level.  Post stratification to species (entered at the
observation level) was used.  This gave me density estimates for each
species per point.

2) Using the MCDS engine, again using a filter to select a group and using
species as a covariate.  Again the detection function was fitted at a
global level and density estimates at the sample(point) level.  Post
stratification to species (entered at the observation level) was used. This
gave me density estimates for each species per point.

I would like to carry out model averaging/variance estimates via
bootstrapping within each of the two methods, but the problem is that the
bootstrap won't work when density is estimated by sample. Can I solve this
by using multipliers?

I would also like to carry out model averaging with both the CDS and MCDS
models if possible, does anyone have advice on how to carry out an external
bootstrap routine? My knowledge of R is pretty limited...

Many thanks
----------------------

messages.subject: Re: Bootstrapping with Poststratification by Species
messages.body_plain:
Hi Catherine, (list)

I didn't see a reply to your question on the list - apologies if people=20
have replied off the list and this is duplication.

Firstly, indeed people do sometimes need to assume a common detection=20
function for multiple species.  I epxect you've seen the paper by Matt=20
Alldredge on this, giving advice on possible approaches to doing the=20
lumping.

Alldredge, M., K.H. Pollock, T. S. & Shriner, S. 2007 Multiple-species=20
analysis of point count data: a more parsimonious modeling framework
Journal of Applied Ecology 44:281=96290

Secondly, if you are interested in estimates by species and by site,=20
then I don't understand why you are obtaining density estimates at the=20
point level.  Distance can't cope with multiple levels of stratificatin,=20
so you can't do the natural thing of having stratum for species and=20
substratum for site, or some such.  But since you're only interested in=20
estimated by species and site then why not combine the two into one set=20
of strata and import data into Distance this way.  So, for example, if=20
you have 2 species and 3 sites, you would create a column in your data=20
spreadsheet for species_site that would have 6 levels (sp1site1,=20
sp2site1, sp1site2, etc).  Import this as the stratum label.  Area is=20
the area of the stratum; lines are repeated within in each stratum.=20
Then, as Distance to produce stratum estimates of variance, but not=20
global estimates.

With this setup you can use Distance to do the bootstrap model averaging.

Hope this helps,

  - Len

--=20
